verdicts.reason: Both ask whether the post proves only one pointwise alternative can hold globally, ruling out mixtures.
Both ask whether pointwise possibilities are shown to combine into one globally consistent object.
Both ask whether a symmetry is actually used to drive the proof rather than merely mentioned.
Identical name and near-identical description of a connected geometric relation chain.
Both ask whether an inequality's equality case is extracted and translated into the requested structure.
Both ask whether the technique's sophistication matches the problem's actual difficulty.
X covers any deviation self-label (e.g. 'a different solution') while Y is scoped specifically to hack/non-genuine framing, so a plain 'different approach' remark can trip X but not Y.
X requires both deriving all candidates and verifying them, while Y scores verification alone regardless of whether candidate derivation was complete.
Both ask whether the post adds substantive structure/generalization beyond what was asked.
Both ask whether a modular/periodicity argument is proved and used exhaustively to eliminate cases.
Both ask whether the post extends its reasoning beyond the minimal answer with a substantive addition.
Both ask whether the post bridges pointwise conditions into a proven global claim.
Both ask whether pointwise alternatives are shown to close into one globally consistent form.
Both target explicit self-labeling of the method as illegitimate/hacky/fake, using the same trigger phrases.
Both ask whether the argument is broken into explicitly labeled claims/lemmas each with its own proof.
X is specific to a parameterized construction's range coverage while Y covers any branch/parity/case coverage, so a case-based (non-constructive) proof can satisfy Y without X applying.
Both ask whether the post proves pointwise alternatives must resolve to one global choice.
Both ask whether the post supplies substantive extra structure beyond the minimum needed.
Both require a parameterized construction/witness family whose valid range is proved to cover every permitted instance.
Both score the same speech-act distinction: asserting one's own finished argument versus questioning or contesting one.

X spans two genres (functional-equation ladders and induction/recursion scaffolding) while Y is scoped mainly to systematic equation evaluation, so an induction-based post can satisfy X without matching Y's rubric.
Both score how much of the argument is discharged by a single unpacked heavy citation versus problem-specific work.
Both ask whether a varying optimization target is rigorously reduced to a fixed simpler quantity with the bound shown attainable.
Both ask whether the post proves local/pointwise alternatives must agree globally rather than being treated as automatically valid.
Both ask whether the post explicitly bridges pointwise-derived information into a global consistency claim.
Both require the two-part structure of excluding/deriving all remaining candidates and verifying that retained ones satisfy the conditions.
Both ask whether a specific trap or edge case is explicitly named and separately resolved.
Y requires a specific overlapping-interval technique while X rewards any proof of full parameter coverage, so exhaustive small-case coverage without intervals satisfies X but not Y.

X is about internal consistency of whatever notation is used (no typos, self-consistent) while Y is about adherence to standard conventional notation, so consistent unconventional notation satisfies X but not Y.
Both ask whether the post proves pointwise alternatives cannot mix and must resolve globally.
Both score identically whether the answer is derived independently of the multiple-choice list versus exploited via elimination.
Y demands the specific overlapping-interval covering technique while X rewards any complete coverage of cases/branches/parity.
Both ask whether intermediate algebraic/arithmetic steps are shown explicitly rather than hand-waved.

Y explicitly separates legitimacy disclaimers from mere style/length remarks (scoring the latter a 5), a distinction X's broader deviation framing does not make, so e.g. 'cursed solution' scores differently.
Both ask whether the argument is organized into labeled Claim/Proof blocks each closed separately.
X specifically requires a recurrence proved by induction while Y allows any justified abstraction (graph, generating principle, encoding), so a non-recurrence abstraction satisfies Y but not X.
Y requires the inequality be a specifically named one (Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM, etc.) while X applies to any inequality's equality case, so an ad hoc inequality satisfies X but not Y.
Y requires identifying a recurrence and then analyzing it modularly, while X covers any complete modular filtering argument without needing a recurrence.
Both ask whether the post states the pivotal hinge idea in plain, recognizable words independent of execution.
Y requires the specific independent-slot/product encoding technique while X rewards any bijection or involution that controls overcounting.
Both score the identical signal (presence of deviation/joke self-labels like troll, scuffed, overkill, different) with matching polarity.
Y requires a named classical inequality specifically while X covers equality-case use of any inequality.
Both ask whether the argument is decomposed into discrete labeled claims each closed with its own proof.
Both ask whether the post explicitly names and closes the specific way its argument could fail (a trap/edge case).
Both ask whether a constructed object's properties (integrality, distinctness, ordering, domain, relations) are explicitly checked.
Both require the post to explicitly name/contrast an alternate or standard approach and position its own method against it, using overlapping example phrasing.
X is specific to introducing an auxiliary structure (graph/transformed function) while Y covers any compact invariant or reformulation, including ones with no new auxiliary object.
X requires both excluding remaining cases and verifying retained ones, while Y scores verification alone regardless of case-exclusion completeness.
Both ask whether a single crisp pivotal fact/identity is isolated and named as the crux, independent of execution.
Both ask whether pointwise possibilities are shown to combine into one globally consistent, bridged conclusion.
Both score whether a named theorem functions as one supporting step in a larger self-built argument versus being the entire substantive content.
X is specifically about deriving-and-verifying answer candidates while Y is about general case-boundary completeness that need not involve candidate verification at all.

X measures breadth (does the witness family's parameter range cover every input) while Y measures depth (are the witness's individual properties fully checked); a construction can satisfy one without the other.
Both are purely presentational measures of labeled Claim/Lemma/Proof scaffolding with closing markers.
X also covers functional-equation substitution-ladder scaffolding, which Y (specific to recurrence/induction) does not, so an FE post can satisfy X without Y applying.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment (assert vs. question) while Y is about whether proposed candidates are verified; the two can vary independently.
Both ask whether cases are disjoint, exhaustive, boundary-inclusive, and each branch reaches a conclusion.
X requires an explicit witness family with covered parameter range, while Y is general case/branch/parity coverage that need not involve any constructed witness.
X rewards any well-chosen, explained substitution that exposes structure, while Y is specifically scoped to symmetry/invariance-based reductions.
X is specifically about introducing formal P(x,y) assertion notation for systematic substitution, while Y is about general notational conventionality that need not involve assertion notation at all.
Both are read off the same self-description evidence -- a route explicitly branded as unusual, different, or a stunt -- with heavily overlapping trigger examples.
X asks whether the proof avoids unnecessary strengthening/generalization while Y asks whether proposed candidates are verified; unrelated axes.
Y requires identifying a recurrence and analyzing it modularly, while X covers any exact modular/periodicity argument without needing a recurrence.

X is about deriving a pattern via recurrence and induction generally, while Y specifically requires modular/parity analysis of that recurrence; a post can satisfy X via a closed form with no modular step.
X is about completeness of candidate derivation and verification, while Y is about hedging/confidence in presentation; unrelated axes.
X measures whether facts are extracted/labeled as standalone claims, while Y measures whether stated claims form a logically connected chain to the conclusion; labeling and connectedness can diverge.
X requires excluding cases and verifying retained forms in a classification sense, while Y is general case-boundary completeness that need not involve candidate verification.
Both score the same spectrum of a named theorem doing all the work versus being embedded in problem-specific derivation.
X is about pointwise-to-global branch consistency while Y is about verifying proposed candidates; unrelated axes.
X is a general necessity/sufficiency-closure criterion applicable to any classification proof, while Y is specific to the pointwise-mixing trap, which need not arise in every proof that satisfies X.
X rewards adding structure beyond what was asked, while Y rewards explicitly stating the in-scope key insight that unlocks the problem; a post can do one without the other.
X requires the specific bijection/involution technique while Y rewards any transparent direct bookkeeping of objects and multiplicities.
Both ask whether pointwise possibilities are shown to close into one globally consistent form rather than being left as independent options.
X is about pointwise-to-global consistency while Y is about verifying candidates satisfy conditions; unrelated axes.
X is about whether the multiple-choice list is exploited, while Y is about pointwise-to-global consistency; unrelated axes.
X is the pointwise-global branch-consistency trap specifically, while Y is general candidate derivation-and-verification completeness.
X requires an explicit stated equivalence/reduction statement ('it suffices to...'), while Y rewards any tailored structural reformulation even if never explicitly framed as a sub-problem reduction.
X emphasizes logical connectedness of stated claims into a chain, while Y emphasizes explicit formal labeling of claims with individual proofs; a post can have one without the other.
Both require multiple load-bearing facts to be lifted out as standalone, separately proved claims before use.
X emphasizes the logical chaining of claims to the conclusion, while Y emphasizes explicit labeled decomposition into claims with proofs, independent of connectedness.
Both are read off the same evidence of explicit comparison to or departure from a standard approach, with matching examples.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment (assert vs. question) while Y is about whether the final answer is tied back to the problem's meaning; unrelated axes.
X rewards any effective strategic use of symmetry (which can be implicit), while Y requires symmetry to be proved as its own explicit labeled milestone step.

X bundles two concerns (fidelity to the exact problem statement plus legality checks) while Y is purely about legality/boundary tracking, so a statement-altering but boundary-careful post would score differently.
Both ask whether the post explicitly names and closes the specific failure mode/trap its argument could fall into.
Both score whether the post ends in confident, settled claims versus unresolved doubt/questions, using overlapping example phrasing.
X is scoped to checking a constructed object's admissibility, while Y is general legality/boundary tracking applicable to any step, including proofs with no construction at all.
X is general validation of any non-obvious bridge (theorem, equality, sign, arithmetic) throughout the proof, while Y is scoped specifically to verifying a constructed witness's properties.
X is specific to translating an inequality's equality case into the answer, while Y covers any target-directed algebra including cases with no inequality at all.
X is a modular/periodicity argument while Y is a recurrence/induction derivation; different proof techniques that need not co-occur.

X is geometry-specific and scores a neutral 5 on all non-geometry posts, while Y generalizes the native-framework question to every domain with its own criteria, so their behavior diverges outside geometry.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment while Y is about systematic functional-equation substitution; unrelated axes.
A pure 'cite theorem and substitute numbers' post scores 0 on X (sole content) but scores 10 on Y (theorem is trivially the primary tool), showing the two track different things.
X is about exploiting the multiple-choice answer list while Y is about pointwise-to-global consistency; unrelated concepts.
X measures rigor of hypothesis-checking for any invoked theorem, while Y measures whether a named theorem is the primary driving tool; a rigorously-applied minor lemma satisfies X but not Y.
X requires explicit introduction of formal P(x,y) assertion notation, while Y rewards any organized systematic substitution sequence even without that notation.
X is a general criterion about chains of invariant-producing substitutions, while Y is narrowly about one specific early substitution yielding a named key identity.
Both score whether the post's substantive content ends in unresolved doubt/questioning versus a settled, stood-behind claim.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment while Y is about whether each nontrivial inference is locally justified; unrelated axes.
X's own description explicitly excludes the case of citing one external theorem that ends the problem, which is exactly what Y measures.
Both are purely presentational measures of labeled Claim/Lemma/Proof scaffolding with individual proofs.
X is about complete modular filtering while Y is about deriving-and-verifying all answer candidates; different techniques.
Y's 0-condition includes depending on/referencing another post's argument even without asking a question, which need not trigger X's speech-act criterion.

X rewards a useful auxiliary structure that correctly encodes the condition, while Y penalizes introducing any auxiliary function/substitution regardless of usefulness, so a well-chosen encoding scores oppositely on the two.
X is about executing the genre's conventional/standard machinery, while Y is about deriving a tailored, possibly novel structural reformulation.
X is general structural reduction while Y is specifically systematic functional-equation substitution evaluation.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment while Y is about degree of hedging within the post's presentation; a post can assert its own argument (X=10) while still hedging on specific steps (Y lower).
Both share the exact trigger example ('instead of the usual X I used Y') for signaling the route is a deviation/departure from the norm.
X is a presentational claim-labeling criterion while Y is about verifying candidates satisfy conditions; unrelated axes.
X is scoped to named geometric relation types (cyclicity, similarity, parallelism, radical axes) while Y is a domain-general lemma-chaining criterion applicable to algebra or number theory too.
X is about deriving-and-verifying all candidates while Y is about the separate pointwise-to-global bridging argument, which can be absent even when candidates are fully verified.
X is scoped narrowly to hack/non-genuine framing while Y's marker list includes broader deviation words like 'different', so a plain deviation remark trips Y but not X.
X is a general necessity/sufficiency-closure criterion while Y is specific to the pointwise-mixing trap, which need not arise in every closure argument.
X rewards effective strategic use of symmetry which can be implicit, while Y requires the symmetry to be proved as its own explicit labeled step.
X requires an explicit comparative departure claim (naming the usual approach), while Y is a simple lexical checklist of derogatory/unconventional words that need not involve any comparison.
X is about algebra being strategically directed at exposing the target quantity, while Y is about completeness/transparency of shown steps; a post can be one without the other.
X is general throughout-proof bridge validation while Y is specifically final verification that candidates satisfy the original conditions.
X measures breadth (parameter-range coverage) while Y measures depth (property verification of a construction); a construction can satisfy one without the other.
X is general statement/legality fidelity throughout the proof while Y is specifically final verification of candidates.
X is recurrence/induction derivation while Y is systematic functional-equation substitution evaluation; different techniques.
Both ask whether the post explicitly and prominently states the pivotal identity/observation that unlocks the problem.
X is about rigor of validating theorem/equality/arithmetic bridges while Y is a presentational claim-labeling criterion; unrelated axes.
X rewards deriving a tailored structural reformulation while Y rewards avoiding any auxiliary reformulation altogether, an explicit value clash on the same behavior.
A post with no theorem invoked at all scores 10 on X (no heavy citation) but 0 on Y (no theorem named as primary tool), showing the two diverge.
X is about proving termination via a descending potential in a finite process, while Y is about pointwise-to-global consistency; unrelated concepts.
Both ask whether the post exposes how the key construction/move was found (plan or data first) rather than presenting it as a bare assertion.
X covers the full standard scaffolding across multiple genres (including induction/recursion), while Y is narrowly scoped to just the opening few moves of functional-equation problems.

X measures breadth of named intermediate landmarks throughout, while Y measures prominence of the single pivotal insight; a post can have many named landmarks with no singular highlighted key observation, or vice versa.

X requires showing the construction's derivation provenance and that its range is derived (not hand-checked), while Y is purely about verifying the construction's resulting properties regardless of how it was found.
X measures breadth of named intermediate landmarks throughout the argument, while Y measures whether the single crux idea is named, independent of execution or other landmarks.
X is a broader bridge-validation criterion covering equalities, signs, and arithmetic in addition to theorems, while Y is scoped only to theorem-hypothesis checking.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment while Y is the pointwise-to-global classification argument; unrelated axes.
X is a general criterion about chained invariant-producing substitutions, while Y requires the specific technique of comparing two symmetric substitutions to show quotient constancy.
X measures proportion of math versus autobiographical narration, while Y measures whether the final number is tied to an interpretive closing statement; unrelated axes.

X is about verifying a constructed object's admissibility properties, while Y is about transparent combinatorial bookkeeping of counted objects and multiplicities, which need not involve any construction.
X is about tying the final answer to an interpretive meaning, while Y is about case-exclusion-and-verification rigor; unrelated axes.
X is scoped specifically to constructed objects while Y is general statement/legality fidelity applicable to any step of the proof.
X is the pointwise-to-global bridging argument while Y is verifying that candidates satisfy conditions; unrelated axes.

X is depth-verification of one parameterized construction's various properties (integral, distinct, bound, relation), while Y is simpler substitution-checking of each of several discrete proposed candidates.
X is about whether an auxiliary structure usefully encodes the condition, while Y is about general notational conventionality; unrelated axes.

X is scoped to a specific failure pattern (an unmotivated guess later patched), while Y is a general criterion that every nontrivial inference be locally supported, covering unjustified 'clearly'/'obviously' steps unrelated to guessing.
X is about invariant/monovariant proof completeness (including termination) while Y is about domain/boundary condition tracking; unrelated axes.
X is scoped specifically to optimization objective reduction, while Y is a general structural-reduction criterion not limited to optimization.

X requires the construction itself be shown as derived (not tuned/guessed) in addition to range coverage, while Y scores only whether the range is proved to cover every instance, regardless of the construction's provenance.
X is about local step-by-step justification of inferences, while Y is about explicit formal decomposition into labeled claims with proofs; unrelated axes.
X is about proving an invariant/monovariant with termination handling, while Y is a general structural-reformulation criterion; unrelated axes.
X is a speech-act/framing judgment while Y is a presentational claim-labeling criterion; unrelated axes.
X is about whether the proof avoids unneeded strengthening, while Y is about hedging/confidence in presentation; unrelated axes.
X is scoped to a single decisive guessed-then-patched step in general problem solving, while Y is about verifying multiple listed candidate answers, a different context and scope.
Both ask whether a single crisp pivotal identity/observation is explicitly isolated and stated prominently.
Both measure the presence of an author sign-off/closing name at the end of the text.
One counts displayed equation density, the other counts hedging language frequency; a text can be high on one and low on the other.
